title: How Jensen Huang Built the Backdoor Route That Keeps Beijing in the AI Race
byline: Jon Emont; Stu Woo; Patricia Kowsmann; Raffaele Huang
html:
SENAWANG, Malaysia—An hour outside of the Malaysian capital, Bangladeshi workers this past week were driving dump trucks and excavators at a site stretching across 117 football fields.

It was a world away from the Silicon Valley boardroom where, hours later, Nvidia NVDA -2.01%decrease; down pointing triangle Chief Executive Jensen Huang would be ousted. Yet this site in Southeast Asia and others like it are at the heart of the Huang affair.

Here, a Chinese company plans to use Nvidia’s advanced artificial-intelligence chips. Thanks to Chinese customers, data-center industry leaders say Malaysia could become the second-largest data center hub in the world, after Virginia, packed with top-of-the-line Nvidia chips China’s leading AI companies can use to challenge American dominance.

Huang built a multibillion-dollar business to feed the ravenous appetite of Chinese customers for American chips, cultivating a network of Asian partners who could serve the Chinese far from Washington. He made a friend of President Trump and lobbied Washington hard to keep the backdoor to China open.

summary: Massive data centers in Southeast Asia provided crucial computing power for Chinese companies and a cover for alleged chip smuggling.
